description: Drive your knees up as fast as you can for twenty seconds and count. That count is a speed test for your hip flexor nerves, the wiring that decides how quickly your legs cycle when you sprint. Slow wiring looks like weak legs. It is not. Find your number.

scenes.narration: Stand tall, feet together, arms bent like a sprinter at the start. When the clock starts, drive: one knee up to hip height, down, the other knee up, down, alternating as fast as you possibly can, like sprinting on the spot at maximum speed. Every thigh that reaches parallel counts as one. Twenty seconds, no pacing, this is a speed test, not an endurance test, so attack from the first rep. Count your total drives, and that count is your number today. Keep it. Here is what most guys get wrong about this test before they even start: they assume it measures their hip flexor muscles. It barely does. Twenty seconds of knee drives is far too fast for muscle strength to be the limit. The limit is how quickly your nervous system can fire the order, lift, switch, lift, switch, dozens of times without the signals blurring together. You just took a typing test for your legs. By the end I will tell you what your typing speed says about your sprint.

scenes.label: WHERE SLOW WIRING BECOMES FAST FEET
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Seventy drives in twenty seconds is where slow wiring becomes fast feet, roughly three and a half clean drives every second. Under fifty-five, your signals are arriving late and stepping on each other; the legs feel heavy and unresponsive, and most guys misdiagnose it as weakness and go train the wrong thing. Fifty-five to seventy, the wiring works at conversation speed. Over eighty-five, you are cycling at genuine sprinter cadence, the frequency the fastest humans on earth build their speed on. Notice the unit: this test does not grade how hard each drive is. It grades how often the order can be sent, received and reversed. That is a nerve score wearing a leg costume, and nerve scores are the most improvable numbers in this entire season.
scenes.sub: under 55: signals arriving late - over 85: sprinter cadence

lines: The psoas is the only muscle crossing hip and spine.
It fires before every step you take.
beats.title: MEET THE PSOAS

beats.text: THE HIP FLEXOR IS A DRUMMER

scenes.narration: Look at the hip joint and meet the muscle this test really grades: the psoas, your main hip flexor, the only muscle that crosses both your spine and your hip, and the one that whips your thigh forward on every stride. But the psoas is only half the story. Fast knee drives demand a duet: the flexor fires to lift the knee while the glute of the same leg switches off, then the pattern reverses instantly for the other side. Coaches call the switch-off reciprocal inhibition, and it is where untrained wiring bleeds time: the muscles fight each other for a fraction of a second on every cycle, like a drummer whose hands keep colliding. Your count is the tempo your drummer can hold before the sticks tangle. The muscle was never the metronome. The nerves are, and metronomes can be taught.

Sprint speed obeys a simple equation: stride length times stride frequency. Most skinny guys chase length, lunging for bigger steps, and get slower, because overstriding lands the foot in front of the body like a brake. Frequency is the trainable half for you, and the knee drive test is frequency in its purest form, stripped of ground, wind and technique. Research on sprint mechanics keeps landing on the same conclusion: at top speed, the athletes who win are not pushing longer. They are repositioning their legs faster, swinging the thigh through the air in less time so the next ground strike comes sooner. That swing-through is hip flexor nerve speed, the exact quality your count just graded. Train the count and you are training the half of the speed equation your body can actually improve this month.

beats.label: OF PELVIS TILT STEALS DRIVE HEIGHT

scenes.narration: The deep dive is posture, because your pelvis is the drummer's stage. If your pelvis tips forward and your lower back arches, the psoas starts every drive pre-stretched and mechanically jammed, like trying to sprint with the handbrake half on. You will feel it as drives that shrink lower and slower as the twenty seconds burn. The fix is a quiet brace: ribs down, glutes lightly on, tall through the crown of your head, and suddenly the same wiring posts a bigger count with the same muscles. This is why two tests on two days can disagree by ten drives. The nerves did not change overnight. The stage did. When you retest, set the brace before the clock, every time, and make the comparison honest.

beats.label: IS WHY LEAN LEGS CYCLE FAST

beats.text: YOUR LEGS WERE BUILT FOR TEMPO

scenes.narration: Your advantage in this test is hanging off your hips: you have less leg to swing. Physicists call it moment of inertia: the heavier and longer the limb, the more energy and time every reversal costs. A bulky thigh is a sledgehammer; yours is a drumstick, and drumsticks win tempo contests. This is not a consolation prize, it is the actual reason the world's fastest cadence athletes are lean: sprint finalists, elite climbers, high-frequency strikers in fighting sports, all built light below the hip because light limbs switch direction cheaply. Your wiring is being graded on hardware that favors it. If your count is low today, the gap between your hardware and your score is pure trainable wiring, and that is the best kind of gap to have.

Now we drive together. Four rounds: fifteen seconds of maximum knee drives, thigh to parallel, brace set, arms pumping opposite. Rest forty-five seconds between rounds. Speed work is done fresh or not at all, so attack every round like the test itself.

Your protocol for the next thirty days. Drive fast twice a week: six to eight bursts of ten to fifteen seconds at absolute maximum cadence, full recovery between every burst, because nerve speed is trained at one hundred percent or not at all. Slow, grinding knee raises build a different quality and will not move this count; keep them out of speed days. Once a week, add strength to the pattern: banded or cable knee drives, or a backpack hip-flexor raise, three sets of eight, controlled, so the flexor can back up what the wiring orders. And sprint when you can, even short tens and twenties, because the track is where this wiring cashes out. Fire fast, rest fully, repeat. The drummer improves by playing fast songs well-rested, never by playing tired ones.

So, your count. Under fifty-five: your signals are blurring at speed, and that is a wiring diagnosis, not a weakness verdict; this band improves faster than any other in the season once the bursts begin. Fifty-five to seventy: functional cadence, the wiring converses but does not yet shout. Seventy to eighty-five: fast feet, genuinely athletic cycling. Over eighty-five: sprinter tempo on skinny hardware, a combination worth building a whole speed game on. Put your count in the comments, just the number, and retest in thirty days: same brace, same twenty honest seconds, same parallel rule. The drummer keeps time in counts, and yours is about to get faster.

Thirty days from now, same twenty seconds, same tall brace, bring me a higher count and we will take that tempo to the track together. Subscribe, and keep your number safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Knee Drive Speed Reveals Your Hidden Strength
